Oracle 0.7925 (+13.02pp). **All signals WORSE than greedy despite 13pp oracle headroom — gap confirmed at 4B**\\n  - SciERC NER 4B gap demonstration: SJ-FK ρ gap = +0.096 (strong correlation advantage), SJ-FK selection F1 gap = +0.0007 (zero selection advantage) → correlation-selection gap quantified at 4B\\n- **n_samples confound control**: Qwen3-8B n=8 data exists as control. SciERC SJ: n8→n16 Δ=0.066, CI=[0.004, 0.128] weak effect. n_samples not a confound for 4B-8B comparison.\\n- **Paper framing**: \\\"Scale ablation shows the gap is not an artifact of a particular model size; correlation strength is maintained at 4B, confirming that the gap originates from within-instance signal misalignment rather than model capacity.\\\"\\n\\n**exp-019 supervised verifier**: IN PROGRESS (D116 Dream feedback — all 3 tiers flagged as critical gap). Simplified to logistic regression on 5 signals (scikit-learn, CPU, ~30min). If supervised verifier partially closes oracle gap → proves gap IS closable, signals carry information but unsupervised heuristics are too weak. Grounds the \\\"what would be needed\\\" part of Contribution B.\\n\\n**exp-023 LoRA rank=8 ablation** [DONE]: rank=8 vs rank=32 on SciERC. Degeneracy: 7.2% vs 21% (3× reduction). Oracle headroom: 16.0pp vs 13.3pp. But ALL selection methods still fail to beat greedy (LP -0.5pp, SJ -0.9pp). Strengthens multi-causal argument and points to trained verifiers as the path forward. Within Few-NERD, per-entity-type analysis shows ρ=−0.881 between degeneracy and LP delta (within-dataset causal effect). But cross-dataset, the gradient CoNLL→SciERC→Few-NERD does NOT monotonically predict LP effectiveness (D154: ρ=0.052 at 23 points).\\n\\n**Bonus finding (parse rate)**: Free-form parse rate 99.95% (4406/4408) — fine-tuned 8B model generates valid JSON without grammar constraints. Challenges intro:19 claim about constrained decoding necessity for format compliance.\\n\\n**Implications**: Not just \\\"signals don't work\\\" but \\\"here's WHY they don't work (intrinsic score compression), here's proof it's universal (controlled ablation via elimination), and here's the forward direction (breaking LP compression requires fundamentally different approaches — trained verifiers, multi-round refinement — not simply relaxing decoding constraints).\\\"\\n\\n### Claim 2 (METHODOLOGY — QE Evaluation Framework)\\nSystematic evaluation of 5 confidence signals across 4 families for structured IE quality estimation. Signal ranking reverses vs NER — structural signals lose advantage when 43-45% of RE samples have F1=0 (binary signal dominance). LP's coarse but stable generation-confidence signal captures \\\"did the model get any relations right\\\" better than structural overlap measures.\\n- Difficulty-dependent signal ranking: WNUT-17 conditional collapse (ρ significant → n.s.) + logprob ρ=−0.410 (non-obvious: overconfidence on OOD)\\n- Temperature robustness: SJ Δρ=±0.01 vs FK Δρ=±0.06-0.09. T=0.7: LP full ρ improves 0.205→0.249, LP cond ρ 0.154→0.185; FK 0.267→0.289 despite more compression → concentrated signal hypothesis (non-tied instances at lower T carry more informative variance). **Paper citation rule**: robustness/temperature tables use full ρ; score compression analysis uses cond ρ. Always annotate which variant.\\n- **Task-dependent signal effectiveness** (new finding from RE 3-seed): The optimal signal family depends on task structure. NER (token-level, graded F1) → structural agreement captures quality gradients. RE (relation-level, binary-dominated F1) → logprob captures generation confidence better. This is NOT a weakness — it's a nuanced finding that enriches the diagnostic framework.\\n\\n**Evidence preserved from original Claim 1** (SciERC, N=8, T=1.0, exp_012_rerun_1024):\\n- NER full (n=529): ρ — voting_conf 0.379, SJ 0.360, EM 0.295, FK 0.267, logprob 0.205; AUROC — EM 0.749, SJ 0.692, voting_conf 0.684, FK 0.629, logprob 0.578\\n- RE full (n=397): AUROC — EM 0.706, voting_conf 0.694, SJ 0.670, FK 0.609, logprob 0.601\\n- ECE (NER): EM 0.353, voting 0.381, SJ 0.453, FK 0.451, logprob 0.706\\n\\n### Claim 2b (Selection evidence)\\n**exp_016_rerun_1024 evidence** (SciERC 8B, N=8, T=1.0):\\n- NER best-of-N (n=529): logprob 0.6501 > sj 0.6450 = ensemble 0.6450 > greedy 0.6439 > voting 0.6337 > random 0.6077 (oracle 0.7758)\\n- RE best-of-N (n=397): greedy 0.4042 > logprob 0.3948 > sj 0.3855 = ensemble 0.3855 > voting 0.3592 > random 0.3544 (oracle 0.5850)\\n\\n**4B selection evidence** (N=8, T=1.0):\\n- CoNLL NER 4B (n=2756): greedy 0.9213, SJ 0.9220 (+0.07pp), FK 0.9215, LP 0.9221 (+0.09pp), oracle 0.9382. Headroom 1.70pp → selection indistinguishable\\n- SciERC NER 4B (n=529): greedy 0.6622, SJ 0.6473 (-1.49pp), FK 0.6466 (-1.56pp), LP 0.6399 (-2.23pp), oracle 0.7925 (+13.02pp). **All signals worse than greedy** → correlation-selection gap at 4B confirmed\\n\\n**exp_016_rerun_1024_bootstrap evidence** (3-seed bootstrap, 1000 iterations):\\n- NER logprob vs greedy: bootstrap 95% CI [−0.030, +0.042], permutation p=0.39\\n- Effect size: Cohen's d=0.038 (negligible), sign test win rate=0.466\\n\\n### Claim 3 (Diagnostic — task-complexity boundary + task-dependent signal effectiveness)\\nThe effectiveness of consistency-based confidence is governed by task structural complexity: compound error propagation in relational tasks degrades the consistency-accuracy correlation on the full instance set, but the signal remains valid within the model's capability range. This boundary applies across all confidence signals tested.\\n\\n**RE 3-seed mechanism** (D073, confirmed at 4B): 43-47% of RE samples have F1=0 (8B: 43-45%, 4B: 47.6%), creating binary-dominated signal distributions where structural overlap (SJ/FK) cannot differentiate quality gradients. Pattern consistent across model scales — confirming task difficulty, not model capacity, drives this boundary. LP's generation confidence captures \\\"complete failure vs partial success\\\" more reliably. 3-seed RE QE: LP ρ=0.302 > SJ 0.265 > FK 0.254. **Definitive binary dominance evidence**: RE LP full ρ=0.266 but cond ρ=0.011 (p=0.86, completely n.s.) — LP's entire RE signal comes from the zero/nonzero F1 split; once conditioned on samples where the model extracts at least one relation, LP has zero predictive power for RE quality gradients. In contrast, NER LP cond ρ remains informative (0.154–0.185). This provides the concrete mechanism for Claim 3's task-complexity boundary: it's not just \\\"compound error\\\" in the abstract — it's specifically the high zero-F1 rate that shifts the optimal signal family from structural to probabilistic, and LP's RE advantage is entirely a binary classification effect, not genuine quality estimation.\\n\\n**MVP evidence**: RE full vs cond AUROC lift — EM: 0.706→0.752 (+4.6pp), SJ: 0.670→0.646 (−2.4pp, 待确认), voting_conf: 0.694→0.642 (−5.2pp, 待确认). Component decomposition shows all RE components equally weak (head_sj rho=0.210). T=0.7 naturally separates knowledge-gap vs uncertainty errors.\\n\\n**exp-005 evidence**: Conditional filtering dwarfs temperature tuning — RE SJ cond lift +0.07~0.14 vs temperature effect ±0.01. T=1.0 preserves more oracle headroom (RE: 0.167 vs 0.131) and diversity (1-SJ: 0.389 vs 0.313). Recommendation: T=1.0 + conditional filtering, not temperature optimization.\\n\\n**exp-001 N-scaling evidence** (SciERC, n=200 subset, ⚠️ needs full-set confirmation):\\n- RE N=16: voting_conf ρ=0.448 (vs N=8 0.340, +0.108), SJ ρ=0.333 (vs 0.244, +0.089), all signals improve +0.07~0.10\\n- NER N=16: flat (already saturated at N=8) — voting_conf 0.401 vs 0.392\\n- **Key insight**: The task-complexity boundary is partially a SAMPLE BUDGET boundary. Compound error propagation increases per-instance variance, requiring more samples (N=16 vs N=8) to average out noise. This makes Claim 2 more nuanced: RE consistency fails at N=8 not because the signal is absent, but because it's noisier and needs more samples to manifest.\\n- ⚠️ Caveat: exp-001 ran on 200/529 instances. Full-set replication needed before claiming in paper.\\n\\n### Claim 4 (D154: Empirical Characterization of Selection Boundaries)\\n**Contribution C (Selection Boundary Characterization)**: Empirical analysis of when and why LP selection succeeds or fails, with DGS as exploratory heuristic (not validated framework).\\n- **Core finding (D154)**: Selection viability depends on LP signal quality (within-instance ρ(LP,F1)) and dataset characteristics. Cross-dataset degeneracy-LP correlation is ρ=0.052 (23 points, p=0.81) — degeneracy alone does not predict selection direction. Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness (epoch ablation, temperature ablation, per-entity-type analysis).\\n- **DGS as explored heuristic** (demoted from \\\"validated framework\\\"): Mixed results across dataset×model:\\n  - Few-NERD Qwen: +0.92pp (significant) — strong LP alignment (ρ~0.5)\\n  - SciERC Qwen: +0.71pp (not significant) — weak alignment (ρ~0.2)\\n  - CoNLL Qwen: -0.81pp (significant negative) — high degen + weak alignment\\n  - CoNLL LLaMA: +0.14pp (significant positive) — LP-quality alignment adequate\\n  - Cross-model sign reversal on CoNLL illustrates LP alignment's role, but DGS does not constitute a reliable prescriptive method\\n- **MBR**: Uniformly negative, excluded. Exception: SciERC T=1.2 +1.8pp under high-diversity conditions.\\n- **Status**: D154 reframing complete. DGS is ablation evidence, not core contribution.\\n\\n## Story Spine (D157 — Triple Contribution: QE + Diagnostic + Prescriptive, Main Conference)\\n\\n**Problem**: Test-time scaling via multi-sample generation improves LLM reasoning, but its effectiveness for structured information extraction is unclear. Practitioners need to know: (1) can confidence signals estimate output quality? (2) can they select better outputs? (3) if not, what SHOULD they do instead?\\n\\n**Existing approaches & gaps**: Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2023) succeeds for discrete-answer reasoning via majority vote on discrete answers. MBR decoding succeeds for MT. But structured IE outputs (entity sets, relation triples) present a fundamentally different challenge — prior work applies instance-level selection (pick one of N complete outputs), which is the wrong analogy for set-structured outputs. We show the correct analogy is entity-level construction (aggregate across outputs).\\n\\n**Our framing (D157 — TRIPLE CONTRIBUTION)**:\\n\\n**Contribution A (Positive — QE Framework)**: Five confidence signals across four families reliably predict structured IE output quality (AUROC 0.82, ρ 0.45). Signal ranking is task-dependent: structural > probabilistic for NER, reversed for RE. QE enables selective prediction: filtering 20% low-confidence instances yields +5-8pp F1 gain (AUPRC 0.70-0.92, VC strongest signal).\\n\\n**Contribution B (Diagnostic — Why Instance-Level Selection Fails)**:\\n1. **Design property**: 4/5 signals are instance-level aggregates → cannot rank candidates by construction.\\n2. **Instance Degeneracy**: 21-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples, eliminating selection headroom.\\n3. **LP Compression**: Logprob within-instance range compressed (0.041 nats). Free-form ablation confirms intrinsic (std ratio 0.97).\\n4. **Multi-causal**: LoRA rank=8 reduces degeneracy 3× (7.2% vs 21%) and increases oracle headroom (+2.7pp), but ALL selection methods still fail to beat greedy → low degeneracy is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT.\\n5. **Capability-diversity tension**: Higher capability → more convergence → more degeneracy. CoNLL 91% F1→58% degen, SciERC 66%→21%.\\n6. **LP alignment as primary predictor**: LP selection viability depends on within-instance ρ(LP,F1). Few-NERD (ρ~0.5-0.7) → LP +1.38pp (p<0.05). SciERC (ρ~0.2) → LP fails despite similar degeneracy. Cross-dataset degeneracy ρ=0.052 (23 configs, p=0.81).\\n\\n**Contribution C (Prescriptive — Entity-Level Construction + Practitioner Protocol, D157)**:\\nThe correct self-consistency analogy for structured IE is NOT instance-level selection but entity-level construction: aggregate entities across N samples via majority vote, constructing a new output from parts.\\n- **Entity construction (multi-seed N=8 mean)**: SciERC +1.02pp, FewNERD +1.40pp, CoNLL +0.10pp (n.s.). Mechanism: recall gain by aggregating low-frequency correct entities across samples.\\n- **72B zero-shot construction**: LP-weighted construction SciERC ZS +1.53pp (stronger than fine-tuned!), CoNLL ZS -0.37pp (headroom-limited). **θ=2/N fails in zero-shot** (SciERC -0.52pp, CoNLL -0.92pp) → LP-weighting is necessary in zero-shot regime.\\n- **Construction effectiveness is headroom-dependent**: Works when oracle headroom is sufficient (SciERC 15pp → +1.53pp), fails when near ceiling (CoNLL 5.3pp → -0.37pp). This is consistent across fine-tuned and zero-shot regimes.\\n- **LP-alignment gating (preliminary diagnostic)**: Probe 50 instances on validation set to compute adjusted alignment score → automatically select construction vs LP selection. 3/3 datasets correct gating. Bootstrap CI: τ=0.3 at center of [0.25, 0.35] stable plateau, routing decisions stable across τ∈[0.2, 0.4] (stability ≥95%).\\n- **Selective prediction**: QE-driven human-in-the-loop — retain 80% high-confidence instances, F1 +5-8pp. VC is strongest signal across all datasets.\\n\\n**QE-vs-Selection Decoupling** (Dream-identified most novel insight): QE correlation (SJ ρ) is stable across LoRA rank configurations (0.360→0.378) while selection gap changes dramatically. Signals are ALWAYS useful for flagging uncertain instances, even when they cannot improve selection.\\n\\n**Headline**: \\\"We present a triple contribution for structured IE test-time scaling: (1) a QE framework showing confidence signals reliably predict output quality and enable selective prediction (+5-8pp @80% coverage); (2) a diagnostic revealing that the correlation-selection gap is fundamental — persisting from 4B to 72B and from fine-tuned to zero-shot regimes — driven by degeneracy, LP compression, and LP-alignment misalignment; and (3) entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation that significantly improves over greedy decoding (+1.02pp SciERC, +1.40pp FewNERD fine-tuned; +1.53pp SciERC zero-shot via LP-weighting), with effectiveness governed by oracle headroom.\\\"\\n\\n**Title candidates**:\\n- \\\"Don't Select, Construct: Diagnosing and Fixing Test-Time Scaling for Structured Information Extraction\\\"\\n- \\\"Strong Predictors, Weak Selectors: From Diagnosis to Entity-Level Construction for Structured IE\\\"\\n- \\\"Beyond Selection: Entity-Level Construction as the Correct Self-Consistency for Structured IE\\\"\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns\\n\\n### R1: \\\"Only one NER dataset — generalization unclear\\\"\\n- **Status**: ✅ RESOLVED. 3 NER datasets (SciERC + CoNLL-2003 + Few-NERD INTRA) × 2 models (Qwen3-8B + LLaMA-3.1-8B) + scale ablation (Qwen3-4B). Few-NERD adds 32,565 instances with distinct degeneracy profile (10% vs 21-58%). Cross-dataset comparison revealing LP alignment as primary selection predictor (D154) is the paper's strongest empirical contribution.\\n- **Priority**: P0, RESOLVED\\n\\n### R2: \\\"Only one model family (Qwen3-8B)\\\"\\n- **Mitigation**: LLaMA-3.1-8B shows model-agnostic effect. ⚠️ **exp-007 数据被污染 (test data leakage)**，LLaMA SciERC 正确值来自 exp_018 (clean rerun)。unified_rho_full.json 的 LLaMA SciERC 条目必须替换为 exp_018 数据。正确 LLaMA SciERC N=8 3-seed mean: SJ 0.325, FK 0.256, VC 0.384, EM 0.279, LP 0.162。\\n- **Priority**: P0\\n\\n### R3: \\\"FK is a strawman baseline — what about log-prob, USC, exact-match?\\\"\\n- **Mitigation**: exp-012 (log-prob), exp-013 (exact-match), exp-014 (entity voting) provide comprehensive baseline comparison. Results: structural consistency family (EM+SJ+voting) >> log-prob >> FK. USC discussed in related work (LLM-as-judge, orthogonal approach).\\n- **Priority**: P0, RESOLVED — results decisive\\n\\n### R3b: \\\"EM beats voting_conf and SJ on AUROC — why present SJ/voting_conf?\\\"\\n- **Mitigation**: EM is a strict binary signal (all-or-nothing match); SJ captures partial agreement and generalizes to arbitrary structured outputs (relations, events). Voting_conf provides granular entity-level scores. NER full AUROC: EM 0.749 > SJ 0.692 > voting_conf 0.684, but ρ: voting_conf 0.379 > SJ 0.360 > EM 0.295. EM excels at binary discrimination but underperforms on rank ordering. SJ is also more temperature-robust (Δρ=±0.01). Within fixed dataset-model settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness (SciERC epoch ablation: −1.18/+0.74/+0.99pp at 3/5/10 epochs; per-entity-type within Few-NERD ρ=−0.881). But across datasets, degeneracy alone does NOT predict LP selection direction (23-point cross-configuration ρ=0.052, p=0.81).
- **LP-quality alignment as primary predictor**: LP must track entity-level F1 within instances. Few-NERD within-instance ρ(LP,F1) ≈ 0.5-0.66 → LP selection +1.36pp (p<0.05). SciERC ρ(LP,F1) ≈ 0.18-0.24 → LP fails despite similar degeneracy (17.8% vs 13.8%). This is the primary determinant of LP selection success across datasets.
- **Structural signals (SJ/FK/EM/VC)**: universally fail regardless — instance-level aggregates cannot rank candidates by construction.
- **Multi-causal diagnosis (D154)**: (1) degeneracy modulates headroom within settings; (2) LP-quality alignment determines cross-dataset selection success; (3) LoRA rank=8 reduces degeneracy (7.2% vs 17.8%) AND improves LP spread (0.057 vs 0.041 nats) but SciERC's weak LP-F1 alignment (ρ~0.24) still prevents selection success → LP alignment is the binding constraint, degeneracy is a within-setting modulator.

The framing is NOT "selection fails" (pure negative) but "we characterize WHEN LP works (strong LP-F1 alignment), WHY it fails elsewhere (weak alignment + compression), and WHAT distinguishes LP from structural signals" (empirical characterization with diagnostic implications).

**Three-layer argument + Capability-diversity tension**:
- Layer A (design property, noted not discovered): 4/5 signals are instance-level aggregates → cannot rank candidates by construction. This is a conceptual clarification — the "methodological premise" — not an empirical finding.
- Layer B (empirical — instance degeneracy): 21-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples, eliminating selection headroom. Within-instance ρ=0.524 (SciERC) and 0.994 (CoNLL) — signals ARE correlated within instances, but degeneracy makes this irrelevant. Non-degenerate instances show MBR closing 23-41% of oracle gap. Selection recovers T=1.0 sampling degradation (LP 0.647 vs Random 0.610, +3.7pp) but only matches T=0 greedy (0.645 macro) at 8× inference cost — zero marginal gain.
- Layer C (empirical — LP-quality alignment, revised D123): LP selection requires adequate within-instance correlation with task quality. Few-NERD ρ(LP,F1)≈0.5-0.66 → selection succeeds (+1.36pp). SciERC ρ(LP,F1)≈0.18-0.24 → selection fails even when LP range is adequate (rank=8: 0.057 nats). LP compression (median range 0.041 nats on SciERC full-rank) is a contributing factor but NOT the sole explanation — rank=8 expands LP range to 0.057 yet still fails. Entity-token LP shows 4× variance but WORSE selection (-2.0pp). Free-form ablation confirms compression is model/task intrinsic for NER (std ratio 0.97).
- **Capability-diversity tension** (unifying insight, D111): Model capability → output convergence → instance degeneracy → vanishing selection headroom. Evidence: CoNLL (91% F1) → 58% degeneracy, SciERC (66% F1) → 21%, WNUT (48% F1) → ~0%. Scale dimension: 8B → 21% degen vs 4B → 10.4% on SciERC. This is NOT an "artifact" — it is a **consequence of capability**, a structural inevitability. The better the model, the less test-time scaling can help via unsupervised selection.

**Distinction from MBR literature**: Eikema et al.'s MBR failure = utility function misalignment. Our failure = utility IS aligned (within-instance ρ=0.524) but headroom eliminated by degeneracy — qualitatively novel mechanism.

### Claim 3 (Diagnostic — task-complexity boundary + task-dependent signal effectiveness)
The effectiveness of consistency-based confidence is governed by task structural complexity: compound error propagation in relational tasks degrades the consistency-accuracy correlation on the full instance set, but the signal remains valid within the model's capability range. This boundary applies across all confidence signals tested.

**RE 3-seed mechanism** (D073, confirmed at 4B): 43-47% of RE samples have F1=0 (8B: 43-45%, 4B: 47.6%), creating binary-dominated signal distributions where structural overlap (SJ/FK) cannot differentiate quality gradients. Pattern consistent across model scales — confirming task difficulty, not model capacity, drives this boundary. LP's generation confidence captures "complete failure vs partial success" more reliably. 3-seed RE QE: LP ρ=0.302 > SJ 0.265 > FK 0.254. **Definitive binary dominance evidence**: RE LP full ρ=0.266 but cond ρ=0.011 (p=0.86, completely n.s.) — LP's entire RE signal comes from the zero/nonzero F1 split; once conditioned on samples where the model extracts at least one relation, LP has zero predictive power for RE quality gradients. In contrast, NER LP cond ρ remains informative (0.154–0.185). This provides the concrete mechanism for Claim 3's task-complexity boundary: it's not just "compound error" in the abstract — it's specifically the high zero-F1 rate that shifts the optimal signal family from structural to probabilistic, and LP's RE advantage is entirely a binary classification effect, not genuine quality estimation.

**MVP evidence**: RE full vs cond AUROC lift — EM: 0.706→0.752 (+4.6pp), SJ: 0.670→0.646 (−2.4pp, 待确认), voting_conf: 0.694→0.642 (−5.2pp, 待确认). Component decomposition shows all RE components equally weak (head_sj rho=0.210). T=0.7 naturally separates knowledge-gap vs uncertainty errors.

**exp-005 evidence**: Conditional filtering dwarfs temperature tuning — RE SJ cond lift +0.07~0.14 vs temperature effect ±0.01. T=1.0 preserves more oracle headroom (RE: 0.167 vs 0.131) and diversity (1-SJ: 0.389 vs 0.313). Recommendation: T=1.0 + conditional filtering, not temperature optimization.

**exp-001 N-scaling evidence** (SciERC, n=200 subset, ⚠️ needs full-set confirmation):
- RE N=16: voting_conf ρ=0.448 (vs N=8 0.340, +0.108), SJ ρ=0.333 (vs 0.244, +0.089), all signals improve +0.07~0.10
- NER N=16: flat (already saturated at N=8) — voting_conf 0.401 vs 0.392
- **Key insight**: The task-complexity boundary is partially a SAMPLE BUDGET boundary. Compound error propagation increases per-instance variance, requiring more samples (N=16 vs N=8) to average out noise. This makes Claim 2 more nuanced: RE consistency fails at N=8 not because the signal is absent, but because it's noisier and needs more samples to manifest.

## Story Spine (D157 — Triple Contribution: QE + Diagnostic + Prescriptive, Main Conference)

**Problem**: Test-time scaling via multi-sample generation improves LLM reasoning, but its effectiveness for structured information extraction is unclear. Practitioners need to know: (1) can confidence signals estimate output quality? (2) can they select better outputs? (3) if not, what SHOULD they do instead?

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2023) succeeds for discrete-answer reasoning via majority vote on discrete answers. MBR decoding succeeds for MT. But structured IE outputs (entity sets, relation triples) present a fundamentally different challenge — prior work applies instance-level selection (pick one of N complete outputs), which is the wrong analogy for set-structured outputs. We show the correct analogy is entity-level construction (aggregate across outputs).

**Our framing (D157 — TRIPLE CONTRIBUTION)**:

**Contribution A (Positive — QE Framework)**: Five confidence signals across four families reliably predict structured IE output quality (AUROC 0.82, ρ 0.45). Signal ranking is task-dependent: structural > probabilistic for NER, reversed for RE. QE enables selective prediction: filtering 20% low-confidence instances yields +5-8pp F1 gain (AUPRC 0.70-0.92, VC strongest signal).

**Contribution B (Diagnostic — Why Instance-Level Selection Fails)**:
1. **Design property**: 4/5 signals are instance-level aggregates → cannot rank candidates by construction.
2. **Instance Degeneracy**: 21-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples, eliminating selection headroom.
3. **LP Compression**: Logprob within-instance range compressed (0.041 nats). Free-form ablation confirms intrinsic (std ratio 0.97).
4. **Multi-causal**: LoRA rank=8 reduces degeneracy 3× (7.2% vs 21%) and increases oracle headroom (+2.7pp), but ALL selection methods still fail to beat greedy → low degeneracy is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT.
5. **Capability-diversity tension**: Higher capability → more convergence → more degeneracy. CoNLL 91% F1→58% degen, SciERC 66%→21%.
6. **LP alignment as primary predictor**: LP selection viability depends on within-instance ρ(LP,F1). Few-NERD (ρ~0.5-0.7) → LP +1.38pp (p<0.05). SciERC (ρ~0.2) → LP fails despite similar degeneracy. Cross-dataset degeneracy ρ=0.052 (23 configs, p=0.81).

**Contribution C (Prescriptive — Entity-Level Construction + Practitioner Protocol, D157)**:
The correct self-consistency analogy for structured IE is NOT instance-level selection but entity-level construction: aggregate entities across N samples via majority vote, constructing a new output from parts.
- **Entity construction (multi-seed N=8 mean)**: SciERC +1.02pp, FewNERD +1.40pp, CoNLL +0.10pp (n.s.). Mechanism: recall gain by aggregating low-frequency correct entities across samples.
- **72B zero-shot construction**: LP-weighted construction SciERC ZS +1.53pp (stronger than fine-tuned!), CoNLL ZS -0.37pp (headroom-limited). **θ=2/N fails in zero-shot** (SciERC -0.52pp, CoNLL -0.92pp) → LP-weighting is necessary in zero-shot regime.
- **Construction effectiveness is headroom-dependent**: Works when oracle headroom is sufficient (SciERC 15pp → +1.53pp), fails when near ceiling (CoNLL 5.3pp → -0.37pp). This is consistent across fine-tuned and zero-shot regimes.
- **LP-alignment gating (preliminary diagnostic)**: Probe 50 instances on validation set to compute adjusted alignment score → automatically select construction vs LP selection. 3/3 datasets correct gating. Bootstrap CI: τ=0.3 at center of [0.25, 0.35] stable plateau, routing decisions stable across τ∈[0.2, 0.4] (stability ≥95%).
- **Selective prediction**: QE-driven human-in-the-loop — retain 80% high-confidence instances, F1 +5-8pp. VC is strongest signal across all datasets.

**QE-vs-Selection Decoupling** (Dream-identified most novel insight): QE correlation (SJ ρ) is stable across LoRA rank configurations (0.360→0.378) while selection gap changes dramatically. Signals are ALWAYS useful for flagging uncertain instances, even when they cannot improve selection.

**Headline**: "We present a triple contribution for structured IE test-time scaling: (1) a QE framework showing confidence signals reliably predict output quality and enable selective prediction (+5-8pp @80% coverage); (2) a diagnostic revealing that the correlation-selection gap is fundamental — persisting from 4B to 72B and from fine-tuned to zero-shot regimes — driven by degeneracy, LP compression, and LP-alignment misalignment; and (3) entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation that significantly improves over greedy decoding (+1.02pp SciERC, +1.40pp FewNERD fine-tuned; +1.53pp SciERC zero-shot via LP-weighting), with effectiveness governed by oracle headroom."

**Title candidates**:
- "Don't Select, Construct: Diagnosing and Fixing Test-Time Scaling for Structured Information Extraction"
- "Strong Predictors, Weak Selectors: From Diagnosis to Entity-Level Construction for Structured IE"
- "Beyond Selection: Entity-Level Construction as the Correct Self-Consistency for Structured IE"

    - Atomic Self-Consistency (EMNLP 2024) — 子声明级一致性 for long-form text; 对比：我们在 entity-set 级别做结构化度量
    - **Nédellec & Xia (Genomics Informatics, 2026-02, PMC12888769)** — "Consistency–accuracy correlation in hard-prompted LLMs for entity and relation extraction"。最直接竞争者：4 LLMs 在植物健康 NER/RE 上研究 consistency-accuracy 相关性。**关键差异**：(a) 他们用 surface-level string matching，自承"overlooks semantically consistent outputs"，我们的 SJ 正好解决此问题; (b) 不研究 best-of-N selection; (c) 单领域 hard-prompted (T=0); (d) 无多信号家族对比。论文 Intro 可引用其 limitation 作为 SJ 的动机
  - **[2025-2026 新颖性自查补充 — 应引]**:
    - UQ for LLMs Survey (ACL Findings 2025) — 最全面 LLM 不确定性综述
    - UQ+Calibration Survey (arxiv 2503.15850, 2025) — 第二篇综合综述
    - Semantic Entropy Probes (2024) — 低成本不确定性估计
    - Latent Self-Consistency (2025, arxiv 2508.18395) — embedding 空间一致性
    - Ranked Voting SC (2025, arxiv 2505.10772) — 排名投票变体，仍限于推理任务
    - Know Your Limits: Abstention Survey (TACL 2025) — 选择性预测综述，与 Claim 1 selective prediction 角度直接相关
    - Confidence Estimation Survey (NAACL 2024, arxiv 2311.08298) — LLM 置信度估计全景定位
    - **CoCoA (Vashurin et al., NeurIPS 2025, arxiv 2502.04964)** — MBR 框架融合 confidence+consistency 做 UQ，在 QA/摘要/翻译上评估。与我们 exp-016 ensemble (SJ+logprob) 对标，但未涉及 structured IE
    - **Vashurin et al. (arxiv 2510.20460, 2025)** — VCE/MSP/Sample Consistency/CoCoA 四方法系统评估，任务不含 structured IE
  - **需新增 Related Work 小节**:
    - "Test-Time Scaling & Sample Selection" — 将 CISC/Self-Certainty/ReASC 集中讨论，明确 positioning：现有工作均面向 reasoning/QA 的离散答案，我们首次在 structured IE 上做系统信号对比并发现 correlation-selection gap
    - "Consistency for Structured IE" — 引 Nédellec & Xia 2026 作为同期工作，显式对比：surface matching vs structural metrics (SJ)；他们的 limitation 是我们的 motivation
- **Priority**: P0, Paper Agent handles

### R11: "SJ+logprob ensemble missing" (Dream 2 — both reviewers)
- **Status**: ⚠️ REVISED by exp_016_rerun_1024. Results:
  - Ensemble AUROC (5-fold CV LR): NER 0.666 ± 0.070, RE 0.662 ± 0.078
  - Best single signal EM: NER AUROC 0.749, RE AUROC 0.706
  - **Ensemble has NO advantage over best single signal** — EM alone outperforms the 5-signal logistic regression ensemble by +8.3pp (NER) and +4.4pp (RE)
  - **Interpretation**: With 1024-token clean data, EM captures nearly all discriminative information. The ensemble's inferior performance likely reflects overfitting in the 5-fold CV LR with correlated features. This further supports presenting EM as a simple, strong baseline within the structural consistency family.
- **Priority**: DONE — write into paper with honest interpretation (no ensemble advantage claim)

### R12: "No supervised upper bound / reward model comparison" (Dream 2)
- **Mitigation**: exp-016 LR ensemble (5-signal, 5-fold CV) underperforms best single signal EM (AUROC 0.666 vs 0.749), suggesting feature redundancy. exp-019 supervised verifier SKIPPED (DDL risk + scope creep). Free-form ablation provides the "so what": gap is fundamental → closing it requires fundamentally different approaches (trained verifiers, not just better unsupervised signals). Positioned as future work with explicit motivation from ablation evidence.
- **Priority**: P1, addressed via framing (future work motivated by ablation)

### R13: "Headroom capture rate low" (Dream 2)
- **Mitigation**: NER oracle 0.7758, greedy 0.6439, best signal (logprob) 0.6501 → captures 0.5% of headroom. RE oracle 0.5850, greedy 0.4042, best signal (greedy itself) → 0% capture. Discuss explicitly in paper. Contextualize vs other unsupervised TTS methods. Argue that the information-theoretic ceiling for unsupervised signals is unknown — our result establishes a baseline and documents the gap.
- **Priority**: P0, paper writing

### R14: "Cross-model validation thin — need more than 2×8B" (Dream 2)
- **Status**: ✅ RESOLVED by 4B scale ablation. 2×2 matrix: {CoNLL, SciERC} × {Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B}. All correlation metrics maintained or improved at 4B (e.g. SciERC NER SJ_ρ: 0.3825→0.4221, +3.96pp). Combined with LLaMA-3.1-8B cross-architecture data, now have 3 model configurations (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3.1-8B). 70B infeasible — acknowledge as limitation.
- **Priority**: P0, RESOLVED

### R15: "Log-prob definition ambiguity — Eq.1 vs best-of-N ranking" (Dream 2 cross-tier, [W])
- **Mitigation**: Paper must clarify: log-prob ranks among N candidates (each sample's generation log-prob), not just score greedy output. Cost comparison table must state "all best-of-N require N forward passes; log-prob adds zero ranking overhead."
- **Priority**: P0, Paper Agent handles

### R16: "Zero figures — data-rich paper with only tables" (Dream 2 cross-tier, [W])
- **Mitigation**: Paper Agent must include ≥3 figures: (1) selection curves (F1 vs N for each signal + oracle), (2) reliability diagram (calibration), (3) N-scaling or cost-effectiveness scatter. Data exists from exp-010/015.
- **Priority**: P0, Paper Agent handles

### R17: "Diagnostic framework overclaimed — descriptive not prescriptive" (Dream 2 cross-tier, [M][W])
- **Mitigation**: Soften "diagnostic framework" to "diagnostic analysis" throughout. Current taxonomy (ceiling/floor/compound error) is descriptive. Either formalize with a priori metrics or reframe as empirical analysis.
- **Priority**: P0, Paper Agent handles

### R18: "No discussion of when consistency WOULD help" (Dream 2 cross-tier, [W])
- **Mitigation**: Add discussion paragraph: consistency should outperform log-prob when (a) model calibration is poor (in-context learning without fine-tuning), (b) log-prob unavailable (closed-source APIs), (c) ensemble/mixture settings, (d) tasks where model is systematically overconfident.
- **Priority**: P1, Paper Agent handles

### R19: "Negative result partially predictable for fine-tuned models" (Dream 2 cross-tier, [W])
- **Mitigation**: Paper must argue non-obviousness: (a) self-consistency demonstrably helps for reasoning tasks (Wang et al. 2023), (b) structured prediction has internal structure that surface metrics can't capture, (c) the DEGREE of log-prob's strength and the task-complexity boundary are not predictable a priori.
- **Priority**: P1, Paper Agent handles

## Venue Fit

EMNLP **Main Conference** target. Strengths:
- Systematic empirical comparison with mechanistic diagnosis (not just "signals don't work" but "here's exactly why")
- Two novel failure mechanisms (instance degeneracy + LP compression) + unifying capability-diversity tension
- Controlled ablation (free-form decoding) providing causal evidence
- Cross-model (Qwen3-8B/4B + LLaMA-3.1-8B), cross-dataset (SciERC + CoNLL + WNUT), cross-task (NER + RE) validation

Main Conference gap vs Findings:
- ✅ 3rd NER dataset (Few-NERD) — DONE, confirms LP alignment as primary predictor
- ✅ LoRA rank=8 ablation — DONE, multi-causal confirmed
- ✅ Bootstrap significance — DONE, LP p<0.05 on Few-NERD
- ✅ Numerical audit — DONE, all corrections applied
- **Remaining**: Dream #3 validation (target ≥3.5), final editorial pass

Risk assessment:
- **Strongest asset**: LP alignment as primary selection predictor + within-dataset causal evidence (epoch/temperature ablation) — honest empirical characterization with actionable implications
- **Second strongest**: QE-vs-selection decoupling (signals always useful for QE even when selection fails)
- **Weakest flank**: D154 removed "monotonic gradient" claim, but the within/cross distinction is more nuanced and honest — reviewers should appreciate this

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We identify three qualitative factors: instance degeneracy, oracle headroom, and LP-quality alignment; degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings but does not predict cross-dataset direction.
The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$). Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.
\end{abstract}

content.content:
1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
13	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
14	On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
15	Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
16	Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
17	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.
19	
20	\begin{figure*}[t]
21	\centering
22	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
23	\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its mitigation. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
24	\label{fig:overview}
25	\end{figure*}
26	
27	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
28	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
29	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
30	Our contributions:
31	\begin{enumerate}
32	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
33	    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
34	    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
35	
36	    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its mitigation. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation.}
    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes datasets.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
Three factors qualitatively constrain selection: instance degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%) compresses the candidate space, limited oracle headroom bounds achievable gains, and LP compression (within-instance $\rho$ 0.043--0.667) prevents exploiting the remainder; within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), but $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is post-hoc ($p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$ after joint correction; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), so this is exploratory evidence.
Temperature disentangles degeneracy from alignment: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve (median $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the selection window narrows as models improve \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), complementary with LP selection and governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) fail to reliably beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}); our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:when_selection_works}).

1	Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
2	All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.
3	Entity-level construction assumes the model produces useful partial outputs across samples; when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 51\% F1${=}0$), this precondition fails and construction cannot improve over greedy.
4	We cover 4B\textendash 8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples (potentially reducing degeneracy), but their LP-quality alignment behavior is unknown, and these two factors may shift in opposite directions.
5	Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.
6	
7	We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
8	The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
9	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
10	LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
11	We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
12	Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
13	The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
14	We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
15	Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
16	Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
17	Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

3	Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage). 1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
5	Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
6	Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
7	All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
8	
9	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
10	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
11	CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
12	Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
13	Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
14	LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
15	Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
16	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
17	\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.
18	
19	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
20	Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
21	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
22	\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
23	Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.
24	
25	\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
26	\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
27	Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
28	CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).
Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.
